facts.claim: "No Better Time" was released on October 27, 2023 by Dylan Gossett as part of the EP No Better Time. It runs 3:45.
Dylan Gossett is credited as the sole writer of "No Better Time".
Gossett is listed as producer of the parent EP No Better Time, which is his debut EP.
In an interview with Holler after the EP's release, Gossett called the project "very personal".
The lyrics urge a young listener not to be afraid to start, and the hook is "Ain't no better time than today". They say sweat on your skin is better than regret on your heart.

The EP has six tracks, including "Beneath Oak Trees", "To Be Free", "Lone Ole Cowboy", "Flip a Coin" and "Coal". The Amazon listing shows the copyright as Dylan Gossett, LLC under exclusive license to Mercury Records.
Gossett released his first single, "To Be Free", on June 20, 2023. He wrote "Coal" in 2021 to help him overcome personal struggles.

Gossett signed with Big Loud Texas/Mercury Records in November 2023, after the six-track EP caught the attention of several major labels. Big Loud Texas is a joint venture involving Miranda Lambert, Jon Randall and Big Loud Records.

Gossett grew up in Austin and graduated from Texas A&M in 2021 with a sports management degree. He then worked in event logistics at Circuit of the Americas. His big break came through TikTok, and his older brother Blake, who taught him guitar, plays guitar in his band.
His 2025 debut album Westward was written and produced entirely by Gossett. "Coal" has passed half a billion streams.

research.lineage: Gossett's music blends traditional and outlaw country and folk, drawing on Texas country and red dirt Americana, though he describes himself as a country singer from Texas rather than a Texas-country artist.

draft:
The strangest bit of advice in **No Better Time** is about crying. "Like the times when you come home, not the times when you're leavin'," Dylan Gossett sings, telling someone to hold their tears for the homecoming and not the departure. Most songs grieve the leaving. This one treats leaving as the easy part, the thing you're supposed to do, and saves the ache for the day you make it back. That reversal tells you whose song this is: someone who stayed too long, or watched someone else do it.

The opening couplet sets two kinds of people next to each other. A quarter in a fountain means somebody still has dreams. A token in a pocket means somebody can't come clean. The song never says which one the narrator is, or which one the "boy" being addressed is about to become. Then comes the line that carries the whole thing: "Sweat on your skin's better than regret on your heart." It's a work-gloves proverb, plain enough to stitch on a pillow. But the next verse shows where it comes from. It describes a face lined by "regret filled days," and the pep talk turns into a warning from someone who has paid the bill.

That's the mixed feeling the song won't sort out. It sounds like encouragement, but underneath it is fear, the fear of being old and finding out too late. "You're not livin' unless you're willing to do some dyin' along the way," Gossett sings, and the chorus keeps returning to hands getting weak and a body fading. By the end that chorus has come around three times, closer to pleading than to advice.

The arrangement doesn't push any of it. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar carries the song, a bass holds simple sustained notes, and the drums keep a plain, unhurried beat at a relaxed country-folk pace. A harmonica takes a short melodic line and then steps back. Gossett's low, slightly raspy voice stays conversational, with no harmonies to soften it. The room is dry and close, so it sounds like one person talking across a table. That's the folk side of the Texas country and red dirt Americana he draws on, though he calls himself a country singer from Texas rather than a Texas-country artist.

Gossett wrote it alone and produced the debut EP it anchors, a project he called "very personal." A few weeks after that EP came out, it had major labels calling. He'd gone from event logistics at Circuit of the Americas to signing with Big Loud Texas/Mercury, which looks a lot like taking his own advice.

The song works because it's pushing you out the door while it's afraid of what's waiting outside, and you can hear both feelings in the same voice.
